author: ChartMasterPro
title: The December Disaster - Mea Culpa
text:
At one point in December, the Dow Jones (DJIA) was down 14.6% for the month - its worst December drop since 1931. And I found myself on the wrong side of the market for the entire month - a complete disaster.
How did this happen? Why did this happen? It was a classic case of getting trapped in trades, holding them for too long, and becoming paralysed by hope and fear - the hope of getting out of the losing trades at break-even (which kept me in trades far too long), and the fear of incurring more losses (which prevented me from entering new trades, or even trading around the open losing trades).
I got trapped in five call options trades (Salesforce (NYSE: CRM ), Adobe (NASDAQ: ADBE ), Activision (NASDAQ: ATVI ), Visa (NYSE: V ), and Canopy Growth ( OTC:CGC )) that expired worthless in December. CRM, ADBE, and V were all entered on Nov 7, ATVI was entered on Nov 15, and CGC was entered on Nov 23. After holding onto CRM, ADBE, ATVI and V all the way down to the November 23 market bottom, the markets rallied and I had the opportunity to exit these trades on Dec 3 with relatively small losses (15% - 20%).
I decided to hold as it appeared that markets were going to break bullish. But on Dec 4, the Dow dropped 800 points, and I was trapped once again - on Dec 5, the markets put in a hammer bottom that looked like a bullish reversal but then on Dec 6, the Dow erased the hammer bottom by dropping 559 points. It then traded sideways for the next four trading days (teasing a rebound), and then went into a death spiral from Dec 14 to Dec 24 where the Dow gave up an astounding 2,805 points in seven trading days.
All this carnage would have been avoided if I had simply sold out of these positions when they were negative two days after entering. That simple. Sure, the loss on the trades would have still been 30% to 40% (the market moves were so large) but I would have been unshackled, my mind would have been cleared, and I would have been able to actually SEE what was happening in the markets, instead of being blinded and paralysed by these losing trades.
It's all psychological.
Perhaps the extensive winning streak that I enjoyed from July to September gave me a sense of false confidence ( the markets will bounce back and get me out of these trades ) - in the end, I was not nimble enough, not fast enough, to adjust to the market action.
Two bear traps did me in - Nov 7 and Dec 3 - on both these dates, the markets looked like they were ready to break bullish - but instead, they reversed to the downside and I failed to adjust my positions (hope of getting back to even and fear of incurring more losses) to the market action.
Sometimes, the market needs to smash your head against a brick wall before you learn hard lessons, yet again.
I am bloodied, I am embarrassed, I am poorer, but my mind has finally cleared.
I still face the highly probable prospect of having four more options trades expire at Zero on January 18 - Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), Intel (NASDAQ: INTC ), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ), and Alliance Data Systems (NYSE: ADS ) - but I am no longer weighed down by these trades - mostly because the market has reduced them to nothing - all hope has been crushed, and when there is no longer any hope, the mind is freed from the object of attachment.
Lessons Learned If you are not willing to take small losses when trading, the market will gladly present you with huge losses. Just because something hasn't happened in 87 years (markets record drop in December) or 16 years (AAPL issuing an earnings warnings), it doesn't mean it can't happen again. The "quality" of a company does not help you when the markets go into panic mode - AAPL, MSFT, INTC, Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ), Cisco (NASDAQ: CSCO ), Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL ), Facebook (NASDAQ: FB ) - all got hammered in December, despite the strength of their balance sheets and the pedigree of their earnings power. Just as a rising tide lifts all boats, a typhoon sinks them all. Trading options without a stop-loss is like skydiving without a parachute - it ain't gonna end well - ever. Moving Forward So, mistakes were made, money was lost, but trading is a constant process of learning from your mistakes. Moving forward, the following trading rules will be adhered to:
Always, always, always use a stop-loss. If a trade is not profitable right out of the gate (first two days) then there is a high probability that the trade signal was false, and it's best to exit the trade and move one - this limits the loss on the trade but more importantly, ensures that we don't get stuck in losing trades for weeks and weeks (this is where the psychological damage is inflicted). Just follow the trade signals - it's not that I didn't have the technical tools to navigate the market tumult over the last two months - it's that I failed to execute. Out Of Darkness, Light There is one bright light that has come out of this mess - my NYSE Bullish Percentage Index (BPNYA) trade set-up. This trade set-up navigated the market turmoil extremely well since Oct 1 - it would have kept me on the right side of market moves, allowing me to profit from both pops and drops in the markets.
The chart above shows the long and short trade signals for the S&P 500 since Oct 15 - only one out of the seven trade signals generated a loss and I have been long the S&P 500 via the Direxion Daily S&P 500 Bull 3x ( SPXL ) since Dec 27.
I am currently in the process of back-testing the BPNYA set-up from 2015 to 2018 - so far the results are excellent - the trade set-up creates more whipsaw trades when markets are less volatile, but the annual results still beat the markets. And once you add leverage to the trades (3x leverage via ETFs is more than enough), the results easily blow past market returns. I should have the back-testing completed this week. The BPNYA could become my core trend indicator, telling us when to be long or short stocks based on the underlying trend of the market.
